item.title: Influence of embedding depth on the pullout of a plate from a confined granular medium
item.description: arXiv:2610.29016v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding the behaviour of moving objects within confined granular media is important in many technical applications. In this work we study the vertical pullout of a plate-like intruder buried at different depths within a dense granular aggregate from the onset of motion to flow around the intruder in the steady state by means of a two-dimensional polygonal Discrete Element Method. We find that the peak and steady-state drag forces depend differently on their embedding depth for different friction coefficients. Depending on the strength of friction the plate may interact with the domain walls, which enhances the drag force until failure of the aggregate, but not in the steady-state as dilation around intruder directs the force chains emanating from the plate upwards and away from the walls. If the inter-particle friction is weak, it is possible for the overhead pressure to overcome frictional resistance beyond a certain embedding depth. This prevents the formation of dilated failure zones above the intruder and changes the failure mode of the aggregate, leading to a slower decay of the steady-state drag forces with pullout distance.
item.dc:creator: Dominik Krengel, Jian Chen, Shun Nomura, Hidenori Takahashi

item.title: Numerical Prediction of NaCl Solubility in Water Using the TIP4P/05 Water Model NaCl/Madrid
item.description: arXiv:2610.29163v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The solid-liquid equilibrium and solubility of NaCl in water were investigated using molecular dynamics simulations with the NaCl/Madrid force field and the TIP4P/05 water model. Particular attention was given to the influence of the intermolecular cut-off radius, rcut, used to identify ions belonging to the crystalline phase. Simulations were initiated from a NaCl crystal immersed in an aqueous NaCl solution, following the configuration proposed by Manzanilla-Granados et al. After equilibration, the system was analysed over an extended simulation trajectory. The radial distribution function, g(r), was used to establish a physically motivated criterion for distinguishing the crystalline and aqueous phases. Specifically, the first minimum following the principal Na-Cl correlation peak was used to characterise the ionic coordination environment and constrain the range of meaningful cut-off radii. The number of ions remaining in the crystalline phase was then evaluated as a function of rcut, allowing the corresponding solubility to be estimated. The resulting curve exhibits a well-defined inflection point, providing a criterion for identifying the transition between predominantly crystalline and dissolved ionic populations. This approach offers a structural basis for determining NaCl solubility directly from the evolution of the solid-liquid system, avoiding the arbitrary selection of the cut-off distance. The results demonstrate that combining radial distribution functions with cut-off-dependent analysis provides a useful framework for characterising solid-liquid behaviour and estimating the solubility of ionic crystals through molecular dynamics simulations.
item.dc:creator: Ra\'ul Fuentes-Azcatl

item.title: Stochastic model of elongation-shortening-switching kinetics of a polymeric filament: Critical slowing down of first-passage and finite-size regularization
item.description: arXiv:2610.29270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Several filamentous biopolymers exhibit unusual polymerization-depolymerization kinetics where continued elongation (shortening) is possible only in an `active' (`inactive') state while occasional random transition (switching) between the active and inactive states takes place. Here, we present a minimal stochastic model capturing only the key features of random elongation-shortening-switching kinetics of a generic filament. The structure and/or function of the filament ends when its length hits a critical value during its shortening; the time to reach this critical length can be formulated as a first-passage time (FPT) and for its calculation the critical length is treated as an absorbing boundary. Moreover, the lengths of the filaments that inspire our model are constrained to a finite maximum value $\mathcal{N}$; therefore, in our model we impose a reflecting boundary beyond which the filament cannot grow. We determined the distribution of the FPT and derived its first two moments. We identify a critical point where the drift of the tip of the filament vanishes making its movement purely diffusive; at this critical point, in the limit $\mathcal{N} \to \infty$, the fluctuations in the FPT diverges and MFPT becomes infinite indicating `critical slowing down'. Our analytical results will serve as the testing ground for the accuracy of the approximate theoretical results of more realistic models for polymerization-depolymerization kinetics of specific bio-filaments.
item.dc:creator: Manvendra Singh, Ashok Garai, Debashish Chowdhury

item.title: Tuning Thermal Memory and Dissipation in Colloidal Glasses via Microgel Particle Stiffness
item.description: arXiv:2610.29389v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Kovacs effect, characterized by nonlinear, path-dependent structural recovery, is a hallmark of glassy systems. In soft colloidal microgel glasses, the stiffness of the constituent particles governs their deformation, swelling, rearrangement, and response to external stimuli, thereby dictating the path-dependent structural recovery of these jammed non-equilibrium systems. To investigate this influence, microgels of different stiffnesses were synthesized by adjusting the concentration of the polar crosslinker, N, N'-methylenebisacrylamide (MBA). The relaxation of the storage and loss moduli was measured using oscillatory rheology under diverse temperature ramp rates, and cryo-FESEM imaging provided direct visualization of the underlying particle packing. While the rapid adaptability of soft particles and the kinetic arrest of stiff ones suppresses Kovacs asymmetry, intermediate-stiffness particles exhibit moderate thermoresponsivity, traversing distinct energy landscapes on heating and cooling to maximize asymmetry and dissipation. Cryo-FESEM micrographs, displaying gel-like networks in soft particle suspensions, dense packing in stiff particle suspensions, and disordered, compact structures in intermediate-stiffness systems, corroborate these findings. Our results demonstrate that intermediate-stiffness PNIPAM microgels optimize structural recovery, rendering them promising candidates for forming colloidal glasses and establishing Kovacs asymmetry as a robust probe of non-equilibrium dynamics in glassy systems.
item.dc:creator: Sonali Vasant Kawale, Ranjini Bandyopadhyay

item.title: Mechanism of delayed elastic state absorption versus fatigue failure in cyclic shear of amorphous materials
item.description: arXiv:2610.29615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study cyclic shear in a lattice elastoplastic model of amorphous materials. The model displays a threshold shear amplitude $\gamma_{\rm c}$, which increases with sample annealing. For imposed amplitudes $\gamma_0\lesssim\gamma_{\rm c}$, it shows slow progression to an absorbing elastic state. For $\gamma_0\gtrsim \gamma_{\rm c}$, it shows slow fatigue and delayed material failure. Our key contribution is to elucidate a mechanistic understanding of this behaviour. We show that progression to an absorbing state maps to single element diffusion on a finite interval with two absorbing boundaries. We derive expressions for the decay rate of the fraction of active elements, and the survival distribution. The diffusing variable is the local elemental strain, which takes two jumps stroboscopically per cycle. Once the value at any site diffuses below its yielding threshold, the element behaves elastically. This leads to a gradual accumulation of strains just below threshold. For $\gamma_0\lesssim \gamma_{\rm c}$ this diffusive behaviour is preceded by many cycles in which cooperativity between elements via stress propagation is also important. For $\gamma_0 > \gamma_{\rm c}$, stress propagation dominates and precipitates failure. For $\gamma_0\gtrsim \gamma_{\rm c}$, the same accumulation of elements just below local threshold that led to an elastic state for $\gamma_0\lesssim\gamma_{\rm c}$ accounts for the fatigue that brings the system to the brink of failure. We evidence this via simulations in which the strain amplitude artificially exceeds $\gamma_0 $ in each half cycle, before reverting to the system's actual state at $\pm\gamma_0$ and resuming the next half cycle. During fatigue, the stress-strain slope $d\sigma/d\gamma$ evolves towards unity at $|\gamma|=\gamma_0^-$, signifying perfect elasticity within cycle, yet towards zero at $|\gamma|=\gamma_0^+$, precipitating failure.
item.dc:creator: Samuel B. Walker, Suzanne M. Fielding

item.title: Construction of highly coarse-grained molecular models for aqueous electrolytes
item.description: arXiv:2610.29653v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Molecular modelling of electrochemical systems at larger than atomic scales poses particular challenges, not least the ability to represent correct thermodynamic, hydrodynamic and dielectric properties while still being computationally viable for large scale applications. In the case of aqueous electrolytes such as those used in vanadium-based batteries with oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions, both a background medium that can respond to localised electric fields due to high-valence ions and control over ion transport properties are crucial to embed consistently in the model. To this end, we propose the use of Dissipative Particle Dynamics (DPD) combined with a newly-devised highly coarse-grained polarisable water model with pairwise interactions designed to produce realistic thermodynamic behaviour as the basis for the aqueous electrolytes found in vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFB). We consider how the core water model can be modified to incorporate the ionic species found in VRFB catholytes and anolytes, as well as how the DPD pairwise thermostat forces can be parameterised to attain realistic diffusivities for those species.
item.dc:creator: Michael A. Seaton, Benjamin T. Speake, Tristan Rimmer, Ilian T. Todorov

item.title: Hydrodynamics of microalgae in sea spray
item.description: arXiv:2610.29719v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Airborne transmission of biological matter is likely to cause numerous respiratory distress in coastal populations during certain harmful algal blooms. While we know that dissolved algal toxins aerosolize, the contribution of particle-associated toxins is still unknown. The observation of microalgae in the atmosphere suggests that cells or cell debris could be a carrier. Exchange of particulate matter between ocean and atmosphere is driven by sea spray: microplastics and bacteria aerosolize in jet droplets, following the bursting of air bubbles. However, current models for particle capture only consider surface effects, which fail to explain how large microalgal cells (5-50 um) can be entrapped in jet drops (100-800 um). Here, we demonstrate with a variety of species that microalgae are consistently captured in jet drops, and derive a new particle capture model based on the hydrodynamics of the jet. Using the enrichment factor, which measures the increase in concentration in the first jet drop relative to the bulk, we uncover two regimes. The transition between regimes strongly depends on cell size. In addition, we highlight the dynamics of particles within the jet and derive an enrichment model based on hydrodynamics rather than surface considerations. This work widens and generalizes established results on bacterial and microplastic entrapment in jet drops, resolving discrepancies found in the literature. Finally, we demonstrate that sea spray can aerosolize toxic Ostreopsis cf. ovata cells. This reveals a potential particulate pathway for airborne toxicity during harmful algal blooms and raises the question of the relative contribution of particles to that of dissolved toxins.
item.dc:creator: Elettra Fig\`a Talamanca, Juliette Pierre, Eva Ternon, Paula Cohen, Maarten De Rijcke, H\'el\`ene de Maleprade

item.title: Closing of density wake in concentrated colloidal suspensions: two regimes governed by compressibility, friction, and self-propulsion
item.description: arXiv:2610.29801v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When an obstacle moves through a compressible medium, it creates a density perturbation. Theoretical arguments regarding the shape of this density wake in Brownian suspensions either suppose infinite dilution or describe only the far field. Here, we study via experiments and numerical simulations the closing of the density perturbation just behind a circular obstacle in dense 2D suspensions of particles that are thermal or self-propelled. In the thermal case, we show that the characteristic length of the wake is a non-monotonic function of density, decreasing then increasing. We rationalise the scalings of both regimes by analytical arguments that highlight the role of the compressibility factor of the suspension. Based on this new understanding of the passive case, we show that the influence of self-propulsion observed in experiments and simulations can be understood as if the obstacle is effectively larger in an active bath, with non-trivial and distinct roles of the self-propulsion velocity and of the persistence time.
item.dc:creator: Guillaume Duprez, Gianmarco Spera, Benjamin Buhl, Fran\c{c}ois Graner, Vincent D\'emery, C\'ecile Cottin-Bizonne, H\'el\`ene Delano\"e-Ayari, Mathieu Leocmach

item.title: Quenched disorder in polymerized membranes: from anomalous elasticity to a glassy phase
item.description: arXiv:2610.29862v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Polymerized membranes are paradigmatic fluctuating systems in which geometry, elasticity, and statistical fluctuations combine to produce anomalous long-distance behavior. In the disorder-free flat phase, bending rigidity increases at long wavelengths while in-plane elastic moduli soften. Quenched random metric and curvature introduce competing thermal and disorder-induced fluctuations. We review perturbative and nonperturbative field-theoretical approaches to these systems, from pure membranes to their disordered counterparts. Early one-loop studies identified a disorder-free fixed point, $P_4$, and a zero-temperature disorder-dominated fixed point, $P_5$. A subsequent nonperturbative renormalization-group analysis revealed a third fixed point, $P_c$, at finite temperature and disorder, governing a continuous wrinkling transition between the thermally dominated flat phase and a disorder-dominated glassy phase. Higher-order perturbative calculations also recover a $P_c$-like fixed point, with anomalous dimensions remarkably close to the reexpanded nonperturbative predictions. This scenario connects naturally with the wrinkling transition observed in partially polymerized lipid membranes. The three experimental scaling regimes of height fluctuations can be associated with $P_4$, $P_c$, and $P_5$, with theoretical exponents showing good quantitative agreement with measurements, particularly at criticality. Finally, we discuss the status of the glassy scenario, the unresolved discrepancy between perturbative and nonperturbative fixed-point stability predictions, and possible extensions to defective graphene and related two-dimensional crystalline materials.
item.dc:creator: D. Mouhanna

item.title: Clutter Noise Induced Phase Segregation in Binary Active Polar Flocks
item.description: arXiv:2610.30008v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Macroscopic phase segregation in binary active mixtures can emerge solely from clutter noise: local, composition-dependent stochasticity, without repulsion or anti-alignment torques. Using an agent-based Vicsek model, we show that clutter noise alone destabilizes the mixed state, producing multi-stripe, co-moving band, and metastable counter-propagating morphologies, as well as a stable phase-segregated polar fluid. Our hydrodynamic theory shows that clutter noise suppresses local polar order and transport efficiency, consistent with the demixing observed in the agent-based model.
item.dc:creator: Pradeep Kumar Yadav, Ignacio Pagonabarraga

item.title: Spatial Control of Compressible Active Fluids
item.description: arXiv:2610.30092v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the response of compressible microtubule-based active fluids to sinusoidally varying activity patterns, using experiments and theory. Microtubules accumulate in low-activity regions and are depleted from high activity ones, with the density difference controlled by the wavelength of the activity pattern. To explain these observations the continuum model needs to account for both active stresses that are proportional to nematic order tensor and the isotropic active pressure. At short wavelengths, active vortices spanning adjacent high and low activity regions suppress density modulation. At larger wavelengths, vortical flows confined to the low or high activity region allow for the emergence of the density contrast. Our work shows that a minimal theoretical model of active compressible fluids accurately reproduces experiments, while elucidating the fundamental constraints on control protocols that seek to tame their chaotic dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Yu-Chuan Cheng, Dimitris Krommydas, Seungwoo Shin, Paarth Gulati, Michael F. Hagan, Aparna Baskaran, Cristina M. Marchetti, Zvonimir Dogic

item.title: CRAFT-{\epsilon}: A Conformer-Resolved Atom- and Fragment-based Theory for the Static Relative Permittivity of Pure Organic Liquids
item.description: arXiv:2610.28850v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The static relative permittivity is an important property in thermodynamic modeling, electrochemistry, and solvent design, but predicting it directly from molecular structure remains challenging because both electronic polarization and molecular dipole orientation contribute to the measured response. Here, we introduce CRAFT-{\epsilon} (Conformer-Resolved Atom- and Fragment-based Theory for {\epsilon}), a conformer-resolved molecular descriptor model for predicting the static relative permittivity of neutral pure liquids. Conformer free energies, molecular dipoles, and atom-resolved polarizabilities are obtained from a GFN2-xTB/ALPB 10 workflow. The molecular dipole is decomposed into chemically defined polar-fragment vectors, allowing fitted corrections to retain both the magnitude and relative orientation of local dipolar contributions. Electronic and orientational polarization are combined with a group-contribution molar volume in the Onsager-Kirkwood-Fr\"ohlich relation. A staged parameterization with 41 parameters is applied to nonpolar, polar, and hydrogen-bonding compounds. For 1393 liquids with permittivities between 1.5 and 183, CRAFT-{\epsilon} reaches a five-fold cross-validated average absolute deviation of 2.40 ({R^2} = 0.93). Conformational averaging 15 is essential for liquids with several polar groups. Compared with an established fragment-based model with 139 parameters, it reaches a similar cross-validated RMSE (3.65 versus 3.41) with about a quarter of the parameters and applies to every liquid of the dataset. The resulting framework provides a computationally inexpensive route from molecular structure to liquid dielectric response and forms a basis for later application to solvent mixtures and electrolyte systems.
item.dc:creator: Simon M\"uller

item.title: Choosing Spatial Resolution in the Residence-Time Approach to Local Diffusivity
item.description: arXiv:2610.29703v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Estimating position-dependent diffusivity with the residence-time approach (RTA) requires choosing an interval width that resolves spatial variation while probing time scales compatible with a local diffusion model. We develop a selection criterion that combines bulk diffusivity convergence with local model agreement measured by the Kullback-Leibler divergence between observed and predicted first-exit-time distributions, and assess global model agreement through independent propagator analysis against unbiased molecular dynamics. Applications to water in a fluid phospholipid bilayer and three permeants in a model skin lipid barrier show that local agreement alone does not ensure global fidelity: in the skin barrier, narrow intervals minimize exit-time mismatch but predict excessive spreading, whereas requiring bulk convergence selects wider intervals with better longer-time predictions. In propagator tests, RTA profiles at the selected interval widths outperform velocity-autocorrelation-based profiles and generally improve agreement relative to position-autocorrelation-based profiles in the skin barrier, while phospholipid-bilayer rankings depend on lag time and discrepancy metric; both autocorrelation methods use harmonically restrained simulations.
item.dc:creator: Michael von Domaros, Rinto Thomas, Praveen Ranganath Prabhakar

item.title: Two-stage Slowdown of Vacancy-mediated Diffusion in a Lattice Gas Model with Quenched Disorder and Spins
item.description: arXiv:2610.29931v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a lattice gas model with random interactions quenched in space and spins quenched to the particles. The vacancy-mediated diffusion is studied in equilibrium. A two-stage slowdown is witnessed in both the mean squared displacement and the spatial overlaps. We demonstrate that the plateaus are due to anti-correlation at the corresponding length scale. The anti-correlation diminishes quickly with increasing lag time. A broad and yet finite distribution of the survival function of vacancies suggests their normal diffusion at large time limit. Our model can serve as a new playground for understanding hierarchical dynamics in glassy-like dynamical systems.
item.dc:creator: Qiang Zhai

item.title: A linear, second-order, unconditionally energy-stable scalar-auxiliary-variable scheme for the CHQ viscoelastic phase-separation model
item.description: arXiv:2610.30077v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The CHQ model describes viscoelastic phase separation in a polymer--solvent mixture: a Cahn--Hilliard equation for the polymer volume fraction $\phi$ is two-way coupled, through a phase-dependent cross-diffusion flux, to a damped relaxation equation for a scalar bulk elastic stress $q$. We propose a scalar-auxiliary-variable (SAV) time discretisation of this system, combining the SAV reformulation of the double-well potential with a second-order backward differentiation formula (BDF2) and a second-order extrapolation of all phase-dependent mobilities: a linear, computationally cheaper complement to the reference scheme's fully nonlinear Newton solve. The resulting method is (i) linear at every time step, with a coupling structure we prove has exactly one solution at every step, for every choice of time-step size; (ii) mass conserving, exactly, as an algebraic identity of the discrete equations themselves (the only drift ever seen numerically traces to the finite tolerance of the iterative linear solver, not a failure of the conservation property); and (iii) unconditionally stable for a modified discrete energy, via an exact one-step energy--dissipation identity. We show the energy identity extends to this filtered variant as well, with two explicit extra non-negative terms. Hence, the scheme actually producing the physics results is itself provably stable for the same energy. A Fourier--Galerkin implementation verifies that the energy identity holds at every time step to within floating-point round-off. It also confirms second-order temporal accuracy, including in the steep-interface regime, and agreement with an independently implemented nonlinear Newton--BDF2 solver. Compared with that independent nonlinear Newton--BDF2 solver, at equal grid resolution, the SAV method uses $2.5$--$3.0\times$ fewer linear-solver iterations and $1.7$--$2.0\times$ less wall-clock time.
item.dc:creator: Ritesh Bhola, Michael te Vrugt

item.title: Controlling energy delivery with bistable nanostructures
item.description: arXiv:2506.14266v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Countless biological processes are fueled by energy-rich molecules like ATP and GTP that supply energy with extreme efficiency. However, designing similar energy-delivery schemes from the bottom up, essential for the development of powered nanostructures and other \emph{de novo} machinery, presents a significant challenge: how can an energy-rich structure be stable in solution yet still deliver this energy at precisely the right time? In this paper, we present a purely physical mechanism that solves this challenge, facilitating energy transfer akin to ATP hydrolysis, yet occurring between synthetic nanostructures without any biochemical interactions. This targeted energy delivery is achieved by exploiting a differentiable state-based model to balance the energy profiles that govern the structural transitions in the two nanostructures, creating a coupled relaxation pathway with minimal barriers that facilitates energy delivery. We verify the effectiveness and robustness of this mechanism through Langevin Dynamics simulations, demonstrating that a bath of the high-energy structures can systematically and repeatedly drive the target structure out of equilibrium, enabling it to perform tasks. As the mechanism operates only through explicit physical forces without any biochemistry or internal state variables, our results present generic and far-reaching design principles, setting the stage for the next generation of synthetic nanomachines.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Ehrmann, Carl P. Goodrich

item.title: Dynamics of self-organization in dense persistent active matter
item.description: arXiv:2512.19867v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider a two-dimensional athermal binary mixture of Lennard-Jones particles with persistent random active forces. The liquid phase of this system for active forces exceeding a threshold value exhibits self-organization with long-range spatial correlations of particle velocities and active forces. We study by simulations the development of these correlations from a random initial state. Several characteristics of the growth of correlations are measured and compared with those of phase-ordering kinetics of equilibrium systems after a quench from a disordered state. The motion of the particles in the long-time steady state is found to be dominated by two streams that flow in opposite directions.
item.dc:creator: Atharva Shukla, Chandan Dasgupta

item.title: Tunable shear thickening in active frictional non-Brownian suspensions
item.description: arXiv:2603.09620v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study tunable shear thickening in active suspensions of non-Brownian, repulsive, frictional grains using particle-based simulation, finding that activity augments the rheology beyond the friction- mediated shear thickening paradigm. Specifically, up to a crossover activity strength, increasing particle self-propulsion drives a viscosity-reducing `dethickening' of the system at large stresses, where the material would otherwise be in a thickened, highly viscous state. Above this crossover activity strength, the system enters a thickening regime. Self-propulsion introduces additional isotropic dynamics to the particles, which compete with the flow-driven formation of frictional contacts. The degree of dethickening can thus be tuned by varying a suitably-defined dimensionless active stress that quantifies this competition. Recognising the parallels between self-propulsion and other contemporary routes to dethickening, we demonstrate that our data, within the dethickening regime, are consistent with a recently proposed universal scaling framework, offering a route to tuning the rheology of dense suspensions. Moreover, using the obtained scaling relation, we infer how the shear-jamming and shear-thickening regimes can be tuned by choosing an appropriate self-propulsion strength, and partially validate these inferences with targeted simulations.
item.dc:creator: Bhanu Prasad Bhowmik, Christopher Ness

item.title: Phase behavior of thermoresponsive colloids drives re-entrant plasmon coupling
item.description: arXiv:2604.15860v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Plasmonic nanoparticles (NPs) integrated within thermoresponsive polymeric microgels provide a versatile platform for the realization of stimuli-responsive optical materials, where the microgel volume phase transition enables dynamic control of plasmon coupling. This study uncovers a counter-intuitive re-entrant behavior with increasing NP loading in which plasmon coupling initially strengthens and subsequently weakens beyond a critical NP-to-microgel number ratio. By combining light and X-ray scattering techniques with optical spectroscopy and electrophoretic mobility measurements, it is demonstrated that plasmon coupling is governed not only by the interparticle distance between NPs confined within individual microgels, but also by the colloidal stability of the hybrid complexes. At intermediate NP loadings, surface charge inhomogeneities induced by NP adsorption promote aggregation of microgel-NPs complexes, resulting in enhanced plasmon coupling. In contrast, when the complexes remain colloidally stable, coupling is dictated solely by NP organization within the corona of individual microgels. A quantitative relationship between plasmon coupling and interparticle distance reveals two distinct coupling regimes. This behavior is rationalized through a phase diagram linking colloidal stability to optical response. These findings identify colloidal stability as a key parameter for designing soft plasmonic systems with programmable optical properties.
item.dc:creator: Angela Capocefalo (Institute for Complex Systems of National Research Council, Department of Physics of Sapienza University of Rome), Francesco Brasili (Institute for Complex Systems of National Research Council, Department of Physics of Sapienza University of Rome), Javier P\'erez (Synchrotron SOLEIL), Edouard Chauveau (Laboratoire Charles Coulomb of CNRS-Universit\'e de Montpellier), Stefano Casciardi (National Institute for Insurance against Accidents at Work), Andrea Militello (National Institute for Insurance against Accidents at Work), Francesco Sciortino (Department of Physics of Sapienza University of Rome), Emanuela Zaccarelli (Institute for Complex Systems of National Research Council, Department of Physics of Sapienza University of Rome), Federico Bordi (Department of Physics of Sapienza University of Rome), Domenico Truzzolillo (Laboratoire Charles Coulomb of CNRS-Universit\'e de Montpellier), Simona Sennato (Institute for Complex Systems of National Research Council, Department of Physics of Sapienza University of Rome)

item.title: Orientational frustration drives enhanced diffusion of anisotropic particles in a liquid labyrinth
item.description: arXiv:2605.23340v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Transport of nanoscale objects in complex, structured environments plays a key role in a wide range of processes, from biomolecular dynamics in extracellular spaces to transport in porous materials such as filters and catalysts. While anomalous diffusion is well established, how particle anisotropy governs transport under geometric constraints remains unclear. Here we use 3D single-particle tracking to investigate the diffusion of stiff one-dimensional carbon nanotubes in a continuous soft matter network of interconnected chambers and constrictions. Transport is anomalous and antipersistent, with strong length dependent confinement and trapping, consistent with obstructed diffusion. Unexpectedly, however, escape from confinement is poorly sensitive to nanotube length as opposed to what would be expected of pore mediated transport. Despite a tenfold length increase and significantly enhanced trapping, escape time increased by only ~1.4. Single-particle orientational tracking reveals the origin of this weak scaling. Indeed, long nanotube, i.e. those with length comparable to the chamber dimensions, dynamically align with constrictions enabling efficient, geometry-assisted escape that offsets increased confinement while shorter nanotubes need to screen the volume to find their escape path. These results uncover an alignment-mediated transport mechanism that decouples confinement strength from escape kinetics, distinct from pore-mediated transport mechanisms, establishing a quantitative framework for anisotropic diffusion in complex environments.
item.dc:creator: Rohit Mangalwedhekar, Limeng Ruan, Somen Nandi, Quentin Gresil, Marc Tondusson, Stephane Bancelin, Lea-Laetitia Pontani, Laurent Cognet

item.title: Entropy functional theory for inhomogeneous fluids
item.description: arXiv:2606.28240v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present an exact variational scheme for the physics of inhomogeneous classical fluids in thermal equilibrium. A joint metadensity minimization principle is proven for the one-body density and the global interparticle distance distribution. The theory bypasses the inhomogeneous two-body density and thus remains computationally simple. A universal excess entropy functional accounts for all many-body correlations in arbitrary pairwise interacting systems. The framework is relevant for neural functional machine learning, for soft matter design, and for predicting hyperobservables, structural correlation functions, and first-principles mechanisms of entropy-energy competition.
item.dc:creator: Matthias Schmidt

item.title: Entropy functional universality: Correlation, response, many-body interaction, multi-component, quantum, hyperfunctional, and Ornstein-Zernike structure
item.description: arXiv:2607.03032v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a comprehensive account of the recent entropy functional theory for the equilibrium statistical mechanics of classical many-body systems (arXiv:2606.28240). The approach is formally exact and based on a joint grand potential minimization principle for the one-body density and the global pair distance distribution. These variational fields depend respectively on position and on scalar distance, which retains the low computational complexity of standard density functional theory. Correlation effects are contained in a unique excess entropy functional, which is universal across all systems with pairwise interparticle potentials. Functional differentiation yields entropic direct correlation functionals that generate entropic response and fluctuation correlation functions via coupled Ornstein-Zernike equations. Two alternative proofs are given for the existence and uniqueness of the underlying metadensity functional map, based on generalizations of either Levy's constrained search method or Mermin-Evans proof by contradiction. Simple excess entropy approximations yield the standard mean-field and second-virial excess free energy density functionals. We describe exact entropic functional line integrals, make connections to the recent one-body fluctuation profiles, and generalize the entropy approach beyond pairwise interparticle potentials via parametric dependence or reduction operators. We also lay out the formulation for multi-component systems, the hyperfunctional for general observables, and the quantum entropy functional.
item.dc:creator: Matthias Schmidt

item.title: Quantifying reticulocyte biomechanics in health and disease
item.description: arXiv:2607.21810v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Red blood cell (RBC) populations are mechanically and morphologically heterogeneous, yet how this heterogeneity governs transport, splenic retention and blood rheology in confinement remains unclear. We combine microchannel experiments with dissipative particle dynamics (DPD) simulations to determine how the morphology, deformability and hydrodynamic interaction of immature RBCs (reticulocytes) shape microconfined flow in acute and chronic mountain sickness. Reticulocyte-rich samples present the three shapes that the maturation literature assigns to successive reticulocyte stages -- multilobular, cup-shaped and near-discocytic -- which we model as R1-R3, each with a membrane shear modulus within the range reported for reticulocytes. A 5-um microchannel resolves these models only weakly, R1 taking at most ~18% longer than control discocytes to cross it, whereas a 1.5-um splenic slit, driven at its own loading, delays R1 by ~30%; both geometries order the models by shear modulus. In cell pairs, a leading cell never lets a follower pass below its own single-cell threshold, ruling out the order-of-magnitude reduction that a wake-"unjamming" picture would suggest; instead the follower queues behind the leader, and a stiffer leader, which clears the slit more slowly, delays it more. The controlling variable is the single-cell critical pressure gradient Delta P_c, which rises monotonically from control discocytes through the reticulocyte subtypes to sickled cells. Set against published rheograms, an analytical estimate attributes chronic-mountain-sickness hyperviscosity mainly to hematocrit-driven crowding rather than single-cell rheology. These results place benign acclimatization, chronic-mountain-sickness hyperviscosity and sickle-cell-trait splenic syndrome on a single mechanical axis defined by Delta P_c.
item.dc:creator: Zhaojie Chai, Jianlu Zheng, He Li, Ming Dao, George Em Karniadakis

item.title: Conformational landscape of a macrocycle using enhanced sampling
item.description: arXiv:2609.18524v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We use replica-exchange molecular dynamics (REMD) to map the conformational free-energy landscape of the macrocyclic drug lorlatinib in explicit water and chloroform. In water a single dominant basin is recovered; in chloroform two conformational states are resolved. We use these conformers as the starting point to calculate proton chemical shifts from first principles and a continuum solvent model. The resulting population-weighted spectrum is compared directly to the experimental CDCl$_3$ spectrum, benchmarking the computational approach against measured NMR data.

item.title: Tangential and normal partial slip at the liquid-fluid interfaces: An application to a small liquid droplet, gas bubble, and aerosol
item.description: arXiv:2604.17793v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: An analytical solution is obtained for the problem of the slow movement of a small drop of a fluid in another immiscible fluid in an infinitely large reservoir with the boundary condition of the normal slip and(or) tangential partial slip at the liquid-liquid or gas-liquid interface. That generalizes the conventional Navier and Maxwellian boundary conditions of partial slip. Normal slip is accompanied by the density gradient in the fluid and is applicable only if one of the phases in contact at the interface is a gas. At the first time the generalization of the Hadamard-Rybczynski equation (HRE) is discussed within the formalism of two slip lengths. It is proven that each of the two fluids separated by an interface has its own slip length. The slip lengths of the fluids that contact each other through an interface are related by the ratio of the viscosities of these fluids. New equations describing the terminal velocity of gas bubble rise and aerosol falling have been obtained. The theoretical results are in good agreement with the experiments at moderate Knudsen numbers, Kn < 0.25. It has been shown that the gas density within a rising bubble and around a falling droplet in the air is not uniform. The relative magnitude of the density increment increases with the size of the bubble or aerosol. Presumably, the best applicability of the generalized HRE should be expected for the interface of hydrophobic liquid and hydrophilic one (water - hydrocarbons, water - higher alcohols, in general: aqueous emulsions, water - lipophilic organic liquids and oils, etc.). These are quite important emulsions in practical terms, for example, for the oil industry and medicine. Experimental methods for determining the slip length are considered.
item.dc:creator: Peter Lebedev-Stepanov

item.title: Influence of BaTiO_3 nanoparticles on the anisotropy of the dielectric properties of nematic liquid crystal 5CB
item.description: arXiv:2607.26263v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This work is devoted to the mechanisms of dielectric response and electric conductivity of suspensions consisting of the nematic liquid crystal 5CB with different concentrations (from 0 to 10 wt.%) of ferroelectric BaTiO_3 nanoparticles with an average size of 24 nm. We revealed that the incorporation of nanoparticles influences significantly the dielectric permittivity magnitude and anisotropy, as well as dielectric losses of the suspension. A pronounced temperature dependence of the anisotropic dielectric permittivity of the suspensions was found at lower temperatures corresponding to the mesophase state; but it is also present at higher temperatures corresponding to the isophase. The dependence of the mesophase-isophase transition temperature on the concentration of BaTiO_3 nanoparticles appeared nonmonotonic. With increasing temperature, both the capacitance and the electrical resistance of the pure liquid crystal increase, as well as it increases in the suspensions with small concentration of BaTiO_3 nanoparticles. Due to space charge accumulation in the shells of nanoparticles, larger concentrations of BaTiO_3 nanoparticles influence strongly the ionic transport by promoting the formation of ionic-electronic screening. This effect modifies the dielectric properties and conduction mechanisms of the suspension, leading to the nonmonotonic dependence of the mesophase - isophase transition temperature versus the nanoparticle concentration.

item.title: The typical red cell makes too little vacuole material for coalescence to build the large vacuoles of pocked cells
item.description: arXiv:2610.22646v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Red blood cells carrying intracellular vacuoles, called pocked cells, are a sensitive marker of splenic function: about 0.5% of cells in healthy people, 20 to 70% after splenectomy. Vacuoles too small to see are common, and visible ones are thought to grow when small ones merge. We tested that idea with a particle model that resolves the cell's membrane, its contents and every vacuole, and with an inventory of the vacuole volume a cell can make. In tube, shear and vascular flows, a cell's vacuoles met within a second, and, allowed to fuse, ten merged into one to five. Meeting is not what limits growth; material is. At the rate measured after splenectomy, all the vacuoles an average cell makes in its 120-day life fuse into one body 0.6 $\mu$m across, the size healthy cells carry, but 16 times smaller in volume than the 1.5-$\mu$m bodies of patients without a spleen. Taking vacuole size as set at formation, a population model in which vacuoles are made mainly in young cells, and far faster in a small minority that alone makes material for a large one, accounts for the published counts, sizes and age profiles and, on first-hand measurements, favours a splenic clearance that rises several-fold as cells age; letting that minority's vacuoles fuse fits nearly as well. At a model splenic slit, the cell's spare surface decided passage, and a vacuole mattered only when it led. A slit experiment would test whether brief encounters fuse vacuoles.
item.dc:creator: Zhaojie Chai, Jianlu Zheng, He Li, Ming Dao, George Em Karniadakis

item.title: Poisson-shot-noise induced escape dynamics of a passive particle and a dimer
item.description: arXiv:2610.26316v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Mean First Passage Time (MFPT) is a crucial quantity that characterizes stochastic processes in various stochastic dynamical systems across different disciplines. The inverse of the MFPT, known as the escape rate, is helpful in the context of Brownian motion and chemical processes. The MFPT dynamics of a passive particle in the presence of active noises presents a fascinating avenue. In this work, we study the dynamics of two different systems: first, a single Brownian particle and second, a dimer (two Brownian particles connected by a spring). In both cases, the systems are kept in contact with a thermal bath and an active bath, and are trapped in a bistable potential. The active bath produces kicks that follow the Poisson distribution. The MFPT of the particle and the dimer is investigated in various scenarios. Analytical results are presented for the small kick variance approximation only. In this approximation, we formulate the MFPT in two scaling regimes: a weak-noise regime characterized by classical Arrhenius scaling for escape rate and a strong-noise regime in which the MFPT scales as a power law in the effective noise strength. For the general case, the problem is solved numerically. Next, under the same approximation, the MFPT of a dimer in the small-bond-strength regime is studied using a sequential-hopping mechanism, and in the large-bond-strength regime, the MFPT is formulated using the adiabatic elimination approach. Motivated by recent studies on speeding up the escape mechanism, the MFPT of the particle and the dimer in the presence of an intermediate barrier is also examined. We deduced from the numerical results that the MFPT can be enhanced and further optimized by selecting a suitable intermediate potential profile.
